>Unfortunately, tournaments shape the daily playing environment. [when was the
>last time you say someone playing a non-tourny legal Mt$ deck?] What happens
>in official tournaments will affect how Jyhad is played.

Actually, this probably doesn't have to be. In Magic, it's just because the
official rules (minimum 40 card decks) are seen as totally unbalanced by most
players. The only answer WotC has for this is, "Sportsmanship - don't build
degenerate decks and don't play against people who build degenerate decks."
Gamers, being gamers for the most part, don't trust such a subjective answer.
As it turns out, however, neither does the Convocation because they can't.
Tournaments ruled by degenerate decks wouldn't sell. So the players wind up
having to follow Convocation rules. If, OTOH, WotC simply printed a set of
rules in the rulebook that were basically usable and play-balanced, I suspect
players would be more than happy to use them and wouldn't care so much about
what the DC sez...

By the way, I haven't really noticed Jyhad players accepting the DC's no-limits
policy for decks any more than they did before Jyhad tournament rules came out.
I suspect this is because the DC does not represent any great improvement over
the original construction rules for Jyhad.

Fred

Why do you insist on saying that we don't care just because things didn't
go as you would have liked them to? We have to think about *all* customers,
and there will periodically be problems that come up where one set of
customers is going to lose. This doesn't mean we don't care about that
group of customers; it just means that some problems don't have a solution
that is acceptable to everyone.

>Yes, Jyhad is/was the best game on the market, but WotC is going to kill
>it, so finding a replacement is necessary. Already have. Galactic
>Empires (from Companion Games).

Great, so go play Galactic Empires. Nobody is forcing you to play Jyhad
or V:TES, so why are you, if you hate the game and the company that much?
Nothing can be done at this point to change the situation with the name
change or the card backs. Either learn to accept that, or move on and let
those of us who still care about and support the game do so. But if all
you do is grouse about the changes and refuse to play with anything besides
Jyhad cards and berate anyone who plays with the new cards, then you are
only helping to aim the bullet you see pointed at the game's brain.

Tom Wylie rec.games.trading-cards.* Network Representative for

Messages.Author: Karl J. Hiller
Messages.Body:
Thomas R Wylie (aa...@cats.ucsc.edu) wrote:

: Why do you insist on saying that we don't care just because things didn't
: go as you would have liked them to? We have to think about *all* customers,
: and there will periodically be problems that come up where one set of

^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^

: customers is going to lose. This doesn't mean we don't care about that

^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^

Your spin control is slipping. Can you imagine McDonalds or WalMart
telling their customers, "sorry, but some of you are periodically going
to get the short end of the stick"?

The biggest slap in the face to those of us who are against the change is
this:

You are not merely choosing between satisfying one set of customers and
another; you are choosing to satisfy a set of customers *who do not exist
yet*. Current Jyhad players are less important to you than potential
future V:teS players. Admit it.

WotC expects that new players will make up for the loss of the old
players, or you wouldn't bother printing the new edition. If the old
players were integral to the survival of the game, we wouldn't be
getting the message, "love it or leave it." Therefore, current Jyhad
players are less important to you than potential future V:teS players.
And that's why we feel shabbily treated.

And there are a lot of us. My group contains seven Jyhad players. We
intended to get at least one box apiece when Dark Sovereigns comes out.
Not to mention that we were three players when we started, and loved the
game so much that we pulled the other four in. Now, we're playing On the
Edge, and none of us is particularly interested in buying any more WotC
product, even when DS comes out. Why? Because you care more about
currently nonexistent players than us.

I happen to be the only one in the group with net access. Maybe seven
boxes is not much of a sales loss to WotC, but I'm just one voice here.

Consider this: there are a lot of Jyhad players out there who are still
unaware of the controversy. When V:teS comes out, they're going to pick
up a pack, realize that it's the same cards (basically), and realize that
their decks will be mixed if they include them. What do you think their
reaction is going to be? Even without reading this newsgroup, even
without one of us telling them how inconsiderate the change is, many of
them are going to be turned off by the new backs.

I'll be watching with a sort of horrified fascination as the new game
crashes and burns. And it won't be our fault, and (for all our
invective) we will be saddened.

Brand

(Disclaimer: You *have* convinced me that changing the name of the game is
a good idea. I do not care to be told (again) that it was necessary,
that "Jyhad" is offensive or too obscure, or any of that. I support the
changing of the name, the packaging, the marketing, etc. I just feel
that the library card backs should have stayed the same, and that WotC's
line that "mixed backs don't affect the game" is bullsh*t.)

--
br...@iglou.com Vice Pope of Dogbert's New Ruling Class

the unexamined reality is not worth inhabiting.

over again, with neither side showing any indiciation of giving ground.

Messages.Author: Thomas R Wylie
Messages.Body:
Karl J. Hiller <br...@iglou.iglou.com> wrote:
>: Why do you insist on saying that we don't care just because things didn't
>: go as you would have liked them to? We have to think about *all* customers,
>: and there will periodically be problems that come up where one set of
> ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
>: customers is going to lose. This doesn't mean we don't care about that
> ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
>Your spin control is slipping. Can you imagine McDonalds or WalMart
>telling their customers, "sorry, but some of you are periodically going
>to get the short end of the stick"?

Industries such as mass retail and fast food have the advantage of history.
These industries have had decades of experience, and their role in the
consumers' minds is largely defined, and everyone has basically the same
expectations for such companies. This is not true of the trading card game
industry, which is only a couple of years old. Should expansion sets always
be limited? Should they always be unlimited? Should there be some of one
kind and some of the other? The customer base is probably divided among
all three camps, because most people just haven't had the chance to decide
what the long-term solution "ought" to be.

It also depends on how harsh a definition one gives to "is going to lose".
If General Motors just stops making cars of a given color, then any customer
that really likes that color loses, in a certain sense. Similarly, if a card
gets rotated out for a new edition of a game, anyone who liked that old card a
lot, or hates its replacements, loses in some sense. If you define "is going
to lose" loosely enough to include such situations, then most if not all
industries have this aspect built in almost by definition. It's a fact of
life of just about any industry with a wide customer base that has varied
interests in mind.

>You are not merely choosing between satisfying one set of customers and
>another; you are choosing to satisfy a set of customers *who do not exist
>yet*. Current Jyhad players are less important to you than potential
>future V:teS players. Admit it.

I am not going to admit it because it isn't true.

>WotC expects that new players will make up for the loss of the old
>players, or you wouldn't bother printing the new edition. If the old
>players were integral to the survival of the game, we wouldn't be

>getting the message, "love it or leave it."...

The message I'm trying to convey is "It's too late to change the situation,
therefore you are going to have to accept it or leave it."

>will. Whether that is, in fact, true or not is still debatable.

Just to make one thing clear: Nobody has instructed me to put any particular
spin on the messages I post on this topic. I am saying that debating the
card back change will not affect the decision to change them because, quite
simply, it won't.

>Wrong. As I continually remind people, CCGs do not qualify for the "it's
>only a game" attitude since a considerably larger amount of money gets spent
>on them than most games. That tends to make people a bit more sensitive about
>things and justifiably so, in my book.

Trading card games should be able to fit the needs of both camps of players:
the ones who just want to play, and the ones who want to take it to a serious
(maybe even professional) level. The original release of Magic may have
poisoned this particular part of the overall vision, but it remains
part of our goal when producing such games.

Messages.Author: CurtAdams
Messages.Body:
"T. S. A. Rule" <tar...@hamlet.uncg.edu> writes:

>I don't think the card backs are REALLY going to change the game that
>much. Here's my solutions:

>1) Require a 10-20% rule, where, if your'e going to mix backs the
>minority has be at least 10-20% of the deck. This can be verified
>WITHOUT comprimising the secrecy of the Library.

This I don't expect to be relevant. For a worthwhile marking scheme, you
will want to mark a fundamental aspect of the deck, (like stealth or +
bleed for a Malk) and that will typically be 20% or more of a deck. Cards
present in small numbers but still useful tend to be permanents; with
those cards timing is not so critical and marking distinctly less
advantageous than with action modifiers or combat cards.

>2) Ok, so what if Mr.Toreador has 8 VTES backs in his 80-card deck and
>you have reason to beleive that these are his 8 best...

Again, not relevant. Fundamental (and thus marking target) deck aspects
are almost always composed of common cards - Flash, Bum's Rush, steath, +
bleed, etc (one of the more inspired aspects of Jyhad). It will be rare
for the marked cards to be valuable. (Freak Drive is the only obvious
one). You could cut for the unmarked cards (the rest of the deck), which
would give you a somewhat better chance of drawing a rare card. It's not
much, though.

> Where we play,
>in the beginning, the Prey cuts his Predators decks... There are many
>ways to cut a deck, just don't get carried away with it... One way is to

>fan the deck out on the table and cut the deck to place the majority his
>marked cards at the bottom... Here the marking sword cuts both ways...

I've seen two suggestions like this -the sort shuffle (where you pull out
all the V:tES cards and put them on top of the library) - and the
selective cut (your idea). Now the sort shuffle will obviously hose any
mixed deck - whether the mixer is honest or not, his deck will almost
certainly end up unplayable. If you permit this, the common idea to
supplement Jyhad cards with the (V:tES marked) DS cards is obviously not
viable. This fits my concept - no mixing permitted.

Selective cut is interesting. Now somebody taking advantage of marking
will indeed mark both his library and his crypt. However, it is very
unlikely that the most useful marking for vampires will be whether they
can use DS cards. Much more useful, for example, would be size marking,
where small vampires get one back and large another. Hence your idea,
when applied to a "cheater" would associate not his non-DS clans with DS
disciplines, but, say, associate his small vampires with his stealth
cards, which frequently won't be a big disadvantage at all.

Of course, agains an HONEST Jyhad/DS mixer, this could indeed be a lethal
cut. So you've come up with a technique to destroy honest uses of DS
cards while leaving the dishonest uses relatively viable.

This just reflects the kind of fundamental problem card marking introduces
to the game. Any anti-mixing strategy applies to both honest and
dishonest mixers, so the honest mixers may well end up hosed even while
dishonest ones maintain a clear advantage. Certainly if you can handle
dishonestly mixed decks, honestly mixed ones will be unviable and everyone
wishing to play DS will have to shell out for V:tES.

Curt Adams (curt...@aol.com)

Messages.Author: Tracy Lauricella
Messages.Body:
>This just reflects the kind of fundamental problem card marking introduces
>to the game. Any anti-mixing strategy applies to both honest and
>dishonest mixers, so the honest mixers may well end up hosed even while
>dishonest ones maintain a clear advantage. Certainly if you can handle
>dishonestly mixed decks, honestly mixed ones will be unviable and everyone
>wishing to play DS will have to shell out for V:tES.
>
>Curt Adams (curt...@aol.com)

I disagree- I don't think that having the backs changed makes all that
big a deal. If your opponent is playing a mixed deck, (and you are
worried about honesty), have him draw solely off of the bottom of his
deck. However, I don't see where knowing the next card is such a big
deal. What I mean is, if a sufficient number of your cards are marked,
you still won't know what the next card is specifically. If (for example)
you were being dishonest, and had all of your vote cards as V:tES and all
the rest Jyhad, you would know that a vote card was on top of your
library. Big deal. I don't think it makes that big of a difference. It
won't change how you play the current round to any great extent. If you
had your stealth cards marked, for example, it may affect things a
little, but it still won't help you know whether or not your opponent has
enough intercept. I suppose maybe I'm just spoiled by playing with honest
people, but when I play, I find that if I try and play so that I'm
counting on certain cards (or kinds of cards for that matter) to come up,
I've set myself on a course early on that leads to losing. I try and play
so that I constantly ask the question, "what can I do with what I have
right now." This is a more aggressive form of tactics, but it seems to work.

--FW

I just jumped into this thread, but I noticed that this idea sort of
follows along one I thought off the other day.

What originally got me thinking was a TV show on gambling. In it they
showed a game of some sort in Monte Carlo. The card decks were stored on
the playing table in a wood box which the players would draw from. The
box was sealed and only gave out one card at a time, and only showed a bit
of the top of that card. Now I don't know the name of this rather bulky
contraption, but I had seen it before (James Bond Movies seem to ring a bell).

Anyways, I was thinking, how about this simple solution for mixed decks.

Everyone still has their original starter box right?

Why not just turf the deck into that box? You could use pretty much any
cardboard box that is small and convient, but the starter box should be
pretty good.

the top would be open, the flap resting ing on the table, sort of covering
the openinglike, well, a garage door, or flap, or whatever. The point is,
you would not be able to see the cards (at least the tops). You would
still be able to draw easily, and it would hide the card backs, and thus
prevent cheaters. It also keeps the cards in a happy rectangular pile,
provides easy storage for your decks, and makes shuffling a deck MUCH
easier that with sleeves.

Well, that is just my idea to beat the card back idea. It is cheap,
simple, and will probably work well.

What do you guys think?

-Chris

Peace be with you all,

I don't like the idea of opaque sleeves. I don't play with my cards sleeved and
I don't wish to. Sleeved cards slide around too much and can obviously lead to
problems as WotC limits thier use in tournaments. I still believe that a card
exchange is a better solution.
As far as pulling from a starter box (pseudo-shoe) is concerned, what if your
deck won't fit into a starter box?? I've got several decks that won't. Just
more hoops that I shouldn't have to jump through to play the best TCG on the
market (though not for long, the way things are going).
